title: THE SAME JESUS WHO SAID “TAKE NOTHING” LATER SAID “TAKE YOUR BAG”—WHAT CHANGED?
paragraphs: THE SAME JESUS WHO SAID “TAKE NOTHING” LATER SAID “TAKE YOUR BAG”—WHAT CHANGED?

Why did Jesus send His disciples without money, provisions, or extra sandals, only to tell them later to prepare for a much harder road? The answer hidden in Luke 9:1–6 and Luke 22:35–36 reveals something every Christian needs to understand about faith, provision, obedience, and the cost of following Christ.
There is a kind of confusion that only comes when you are genuinely trying to obey God.
You read one passage of Scripture, and Jesus says, “Take nothing.”
Then you turn a few chapters, and the same Jesus says, “Take a purse.”
And suddenly, a question begins forming in your heart.
Did Jesus change His mind?
Was the first command only temporary?
Does trusting God mean refusing to prepare for tomorrow? Or does preparing for tomorrow mean you have stopped trusting Him?

And if you have ever been down to your last few pesos, stared at unpaid bills, worried about feeding your children, or wondered whether making practical preparations meant you were lacking faith, this question is far more personal than it first appears.
Because underneath the question about money bags and sandals is something much deeper.
What does obedience look like when God leads you into a season that looks nothing like the one before it?
The answer begins on a dusty road in Galilee.
Jesus had called twelve ordinary men to follow Him.

They were not wealthy religious celebrities. They were fishermen, a tax collector, and men whose lives had been interrupted by a Carpenter from Nazareth who spoke with an authority no one could explain away.
They had watched Him touch lepers.
They had seen demons flee.
They had witnessed storms become quiet at His command.
And now, the One they had followed was sending them out.
Luke 9:1–3 tells us that Jesus gave the Twelve power and authority over demons and diseases and sent them to proclaim the kingdom of God and heal the sick.
Then came an astonishing instruction.
“Take nothing for your journey, neither staves, nor scrip, neither bread, neither money; neither have two coats apiece.” (Luke 9:3, KJV)
Nothing.
No bread packed for emergencies.
No money hidden away just in case.
No travel bag filled with supplies.
No extra tunic.
Not even a walking staff, according to Luke's account.
Jesus was sending them into villages with a message powerful enough to change eternity, yet He was stripping away the ordinary provisions a traveler would naturally want to carry.
Imagine being one of those disciples.
You are standing before the Lord, listening carefully, and wondering whether you heard Him correctly.
“Lord, what happens when we get hungry?”
“What if nobody welcomes us?”
“What if we need something we did not bring?”
Scripture does not record those particular questions. But anyone who has ever faced an uncertain tomorrow knows how naturally they arise.
And here is what makes this moment so extraordinary.
Jesus was not sending them without resources because He had forgotten their needs.
He was teaching them to depend upon the provision that would accompany His assignment.
The Greek wording of Luke 9:3 makes the command especially striking.
Μηδὲν αἴρετε εἰς τὴν ὁδόν.
Mēden airete eis tēn hodon.
“Take nothing for the journey.”
The word μηδέν (mēden) means “nothing.”
The instruction was direct.
But notice something important.
Jesus did not say, “You will never need practical resources again.”
He was giving specific instructions for a specific mission.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because when we turn a temporary command into a universal rule, we can burden believers with expectations Jesus never imposed upon every journey.

The disciples were being sent among the people of Israel, announcing that the kingdom of God had drawn near. They were to receive hospitality where they were welcomed and move on where they were rejected.
Their dependence would become part of their training.
They would learn that the success of their mission did not ultimately rest upon the weight of their luggage or the amount of money in their hands.
It rested upon the authority of the One who sent them.
And there is something deeply comforting about that.
Because perhaps you are reading this while carrying a burden nobody else can see.
You are doing your best.
You are praying.
You are trying to remain faithful.
But your resources are painfully limited.
You have responsibilities that will not disappear simply because you quote a Bible verse.
You have people depending on you.
And sometimes you wonder whether God sees how close you are to running out.
The disciples' journey reminds us that Jesus knew their needs before they stepped onto the road.
But the story does not end there.
And this is where many readers miss the turning point.
In Luke 22, the atmosphere is completely different.
The crowds that once welcomed Jesus are no longer the center of the story.
The cross is approaching.
Betrayal is already moving through the darkness.
Jesus is sharing His final meal with His disciples before His arrest.
And in that solemn setting, He asks a question that reaches backward into their earlier experience.
“When I sent you without purse, and scrip, and shoes, lacked ye any thing?”
They answered:
“Nothing.” (Luke 22:35, KJV)
Stop there.
Let that answer settle into your heart.
Nothing.
They had traveled without the usual supplies, and looking back, they could testify that their needs had been met.
Jesus was not asking because He had forgotten what happened.
He was drawing their attention to what they had experienced.
He wanted them to remember.
The same Lord who had sent them out had not abandoned them on the road.
Then, immediately after reminding them of His provision, Jesus said something unexpected.
“But now, he that hath a purse, let him take it, and likewise his scrip...” (Luke 22:36, KJV)
But now.
Two words that change the entire situation.
In Greek, Luke records:
ἀλλὰ νῦν
Alla nyn.
“But now.”
The contrast is unmistakable.
Previously, they were sent under one set of instructions.
Now, as Jesus approached His suffering and the disciples faced a new phase of their mission, He gave different instructions.
And the change was not a contradiction.
It was a change in circumstances.
The disciples were moving toward a world in which their Master would be arrested, condemned, crucified, and raised from the dead.
They would eventually proclaim His resurrection in places where opposition could become severe.
They would face rejection, persecution, imprisonment, and hardship.
The earlier journey had taught them dependence.
The coming journeys would require dependence alongside practical preparation.
Jesus was not telling them to exchange faith for money.
He was teaching them that faithfulness does not always look identical in every season.
The command changed because the circumstances of the mission changed. The Lord who gave the command did not change.
That truth deserves to be remembered.
Because some Christians have been made to feel guilty for saving money.
Others have been told that buying insurance, preparing food, planning for their families, or setting aside emergency funds proves they do not trust God.
And still others have made the opposite mistake, believing that sufficient resources can guarantee safety, success, and freedom from suffering.
Scripture supports neither extreme.
Proverbs 6:6–8 praises the ant for preparing its food.
Proverbs 21:5 commends diligent planning.
Paul instructs believers to care responsibly for their households in 1 Timothy 5:8.
Yet Jesus also warns against storing up treasures as though earthly wealth could become our ultimate security (Matthew 6:19–21).
And He teaches us not to be consumed by anxiety about tomorrow (Matthew 6:25–34).
Preparation and trust are not enemies.
They become enemies only when preparation replaces trust, or when a distorted idea of trust becomes an excuse for neglecting responsibility.
A Christian may save money while trusting God.
A Christian may travel with provisions while trusting God.
A Christian may work diligently, budget carefully, and prepare for emergencies while trusting God.
And a Christian who has no savings at all is not thereby less loved by God.
The question is not simply what is inside your bag.
The question is what has taken possession of your heart.
Do you trust the money more than the Lord who provides the ability to earn it?
Or do you recognize that every resource you possess is something to steward under His authority?
But there is another detail in these passages that deserves careful attention.
The sandals.
Luke 9:3 specifically forbids carrying certain supplies, but it does not explicitly tell the disciples to travel barefoot.
Luke 22:35, however, refers to their earlier journey as one undertaken without a purse, travel bag, and shoes or sandals.
Matthew 10:10 likewise includes footwear among the provisions not to be acquired for that mission, while Mark 6:9 specifically permits the disciples to wear sandals.
At first glance, these details can seem difficult to reconcile.
But the accounts distinguish between what a traveler wore and what he was to acquire or carry as additional equipment.
Mark explicitly says they were to wear sandals, while the emphasis in Matthew and Luke is on not securing extra provisions for the journey.
We should be careful not to pretend that every wording difference disappears without interpretation. The Gospel accounts emphasize the instructions from somewhat different angles.
Yet they share a clear central message.
The disciples were not to make their mission dependent upon accumulating travel supplies.
And when Jesus later instructed them to take a purse and bag, He was preparing them for a different stage of service.
The lesson was never that holiness depends on whether you wear sandals.
The lesson was obedience to Jesus.
And that brings us to the most misunderstood part of Luke 22.
The sword.
Jesus continues:
“And he that hath no sword, let him sell his garment, and buy one.” (Luke 22:36, KJV)
Some readers stop there and conclude that Jesus was establishing a universal command for Christians to arm themselves.
Others insist that the sword must be entirely figurative.
But the surrounding context requires more careful reading.
In Luke 22:37, Jesus immediately explains that Scripture concerning His being numbered with transgressors is reaching its fulfillment, drawing from Isaiah 53:12.
The disciples then say:
“Lord, behold, here are two swords.”
Jesus answers:
“It is enough.” (Luke 22:38, KJV)
The Greek phrase is:
Ἱκανόν ἐστιν.
Hikanon estin.
“It is enough.”
Interpreters disagree about whether Jesus meant that two swords were sufficient for the immediate situation or that the disciples had misunderstood Him and the conversation should end.
But the events that follow place a firm boundary around any interpretation.
When Jesus is arrested and one of His followers strikes the high priest's servant, Jesus intervenes.
He stops the violence.
He heals the injured man.
Luke 22:51 records His words:
“Suffer ye thus far.”
And in Matthew 26:52, Jesus warns:
“All they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.”
Whatever the full significance of the sword instruction in Luke 22:36, it cannot rightly be used to justify violent resistance to Jesus' arrest or the advancement of His kingdom through force.
The kingdom of Christ does not spread through coercion.
The Gospel is not made powerful by a weapon.
Its power rests in the crucified and risen Savior.
And now the story becomes painfully beautiful.
Because the disciples were being told to prepare for difficult journeys, but Jesus Himself was preparing to walk a road no one else could walk for them.
They were concerned about bags.
He was approaching betrayal.
They were thinking about swords.
He was preparing to surrender Himself.
They were trying to understand how to survive the coming darkness.
He was about to enter that darkness to accomplish their redemption.
And this is where the passage becomes more than a discussion about travel equipment.
It becomes a window into the heart of the Gospel.
The same Jesus who cared whether His disciples had enough to eat was about to give His own body for sinners.
The same Jesus who remembered their practical needs was about to bear the immeasurably greater burden of human sin.
The same Jesus who sent them to announce the kingdom was about to open the way into that kingdom through His death and resurrection.
And among those disciples was Peter.
Peter, who had walked with Jesus.
Peter, who had witnessed miracles.
Peter, who had confidently declared his loyalty.
Peter, who would soon deny even knowing Him.
Imagine that.
A man could carry the right bag, wear the right sandals, possess the right equipment, and still discover that his greatest weakness was not what he lacked in his hands.
It was what was happening inside his heart.
And perhaps that is where this story finds you.
You have tried to prepare for everything.
You have planned your future.
You have worked hard.
You have protected your reputation.
You have built routines that make you feel secure.
But there are things no amount of money can fix.
A marriage growing cold.
A child who no longer wants to speak to you.
A secret sin you keep promising to abandon.
A painful memory that returns when the room becomes quiet.
A fear that everyone sees your Christian appearance but nobody knows your private battles.
And sometimes the hardest thing to admit is that you can have everything packed for tomorrow and still feel completely unprepared to face yourself today.
Peter knew something about that.
After denying Jesus, he went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:62).
The confident disciple had become a broken man.
And yet his failure was not the final chapter.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and commissioned him to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
That restoration was not permission to treat sin lightly.
It was grace meeting a repentant, humbled disciple.
It was the risen Christ calling a fallen man back into faithful service.
Peter's denial was real. But so was Jesus' mercy.
And that is the Gospel's scandalous beauty.
We do not earn redemption by packing the perfect bag of religious achievements.
We do not purchase forgiveness with good works.
We cannot prepare enough, perform enough, or give enough money to erase our sins.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
And the grace that saves us does not leave us unchanged.
Ephesians 2:10 immediately reminds us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace produces a new direction.
Forgiveness opens the door to repentance.
And genuine faith begins to reshape the way we live.
So when Jesus says, “Take nothing,” and later says, “But now, take a purse,” we are not witnessing a Savior who cannot decide what He wants.
We are witnessing a Savior who knows exactly what His disciples need for each assignment.
Sometimes He teaches them to go with less.
Sometimes He teaches them to prepare with more.
In both situations, the deepest call remains the same.
Trust Me.
Obey Me.
And never confuse the provision with the Provider.
Perhaps your life has changed in ways you never expected.
There was a season when everything seemed to come easily.
Doors opened.
People helped.
Your prayers seemed to receive answers almost immediately.
Then came another season.
The bills increased.
The opportunities disappeared.
The people you counted on walked away.
The same road that once felt peaceful became difficult.
And you began wondering whether God had changed.
But changing circumstances are not proof of a changing Savior.
Hebrews 13:8 declares:
“Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.”
His instructions may address different circumstances.
His character remains faithful.
His holiness does not weaken.
His compassion does not expire.
His promises do not become worthless when life becomes hard.
And His grace is not reserved for people whose lives have never fallen apart.
If you are walking through a season of uncertainty, do not mistake every hardship for divine punishment.
Do not assume that financial difficulty automatically means you have disobeyed God.
Do not assume that financial prosperity automatically proves you are pleasing Him.
The apostles themselves experienced both provision and severe deprivation.
Paul could speak of knowing how to live with abundance and how to suffer need (Philippians 4:12–13).
And his confidence in Christ did not mean that he would never experience hunger.
It meant Christ would strengthen him to remain faithful through changing circumstances.
That is a much deeper faith than the promise of a comfortable life.
It is faith that can survive when comfort disappears.
And maybe today, you need to stop asking only, “Lord, why has my situation changed?”
And begin asking, “Lord, how do You want me to obey You in this situation?”
That question can change the way you face tomorrow.
If you need to prepare, prepare wisely.
If you need to ask for help, do not let pride silence you.
If you need to repent, do not delay.
If you need to forgive someone, bring that struggle honestly before Christ.
If you need to release your grip on money because it has become your security, remember that earthly possessions cannot carry the weight of your soul.
And if you are exhausted from trying to prove that you are strong enough, remember that the Savior who restored Peter already knows the truth about human weakness.
You do not need to pretend before Him.
You need to come to Him.
With your questions.
With your failures.
With your fears.
With your unfinished story.
Jesus does not promise that every journey will be easy.
But He has demonstrated His love decisively at the cross.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we learned to hide every weakness.
Not after we had enough money to feel secure.
While we were still sinners.
That is why the message of Jesus Christ deserves more than casual admiration.
It calls for repentance, faith, surrender, and a transformed life.
And it is why we continue sharing the Gospel through Gospel Warrior.
Not because a Facebook page can save anyone.
And certainly not because giving money makes someone more righteous before God.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
But the truth about Him is worth proclaiming.
Every article that reaches a weary believer, every biblical resource that helps someone understand Scripture, every devotional that points a struggling soul back to Christ is an opportunity to serve.
These resources are offered to encourage believers, equip families, strengthen discipleship, and help people engage with biblical truth.
And keeping this work going requires real time, effort, resources, and faithful stewardship.
Think of it as a voluntary, recurring ministry offering—an opportunity to set aside part of your giving to support the continued creation and expansion of Gospel-centered resources.
It is not a replacement for every believer's responsibilities to their local church, nor is it a requirement for receiving God's blessing.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, purposeful, and free from compulsion.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Not fear.
Not guilt.
But love for Christ, gratitude for His grace, and a desire to help make biblical teaching accessible to more people.
The deeper reason is the opportunity to participate in something that points beyond ourselves.
You are not less valuable.
You are not less faithful.
And you are not excluded from the encouragement and biblical truth we share.
There is another meaningful way you can help.
You never know who is reading quietly.
Someone may be questioning God's faithfulness because their finances have collapsed.
Someone may be carrying guilt over a failure they believe is unforgivable.
Someone may have misunderstood Scripture and quietly walked away from faith.
Someone may simply need to be reminded that the Jesus who called Peter did not abandon him after his worst night.
One thoughtful share can place the message of Christ before someone you could never reach in person.
And if this message has reached something personal in your heart, I would love for you to join the conversation.
Or, if you are walking through a particularly difficult chapter, simply comment, “Pray for me.”
You do not have to explain everything publicly.
You do not have to expose private pain to prove your faith.
But sometimes even a few honest words can remind another struggling believer that they are not the only one fighting to remain faithful.
It is not ultimately about money bags.
It is not ultimately about sandals.
It is not even ultimately about how much preparation you should make for your next journey.
It is about the Lord who sends His people, teaches them through changing circumstances, and remains worthy of their trust.
The disciples once walked into villages carrying almost nothing.
Later, they would carry provisions into a world where following Jesus could cost them everything.
But after the resurrection, they carried something infinitely more important than either a purse or a travel bag.
They carried the testimony that Jesus Christ had conquered death.
They proclaimed forgiveness of sins in His name.
They called people to repent and believe.
And they bore witness to a Savior whose kingdom could not be defeated by the very cross His enemies had used against Him.
That is the message we must never lose.
Not a Gospel of guaranteed wealth.
Not a Gospel of effortless living.
Not a Gospel in which generosity purchases divine approval.
But the Gospel of Jesus Christ—crucified for sinners, risen in victory, calling the lost to repentance and offering forgiveness and new life through faith in Him.
The same Lord who instructed the disciples to travel without a bag later told them to take one.
And both commands came from the same faithful Savior.
So prepare wisely when preparation is needed.
Depend upon God in every circumstance.
Hold your possessions with open hands.
Obey the Word of Christ in its proper context.
And when you stumble, do not run farther into the darkness.
Return to the One who restores repentant sinners.
Because the greatest tragedy is not reaching the end of a road with an empty money bag.
It is reaching the end of your life with a heart that never surrendered to Jesus.
And the greatest miracle is not that the disciples survived their journeys without provisions.
It is that the Son of God willingly went to the cross, rose from the grave, and opened the way for sinners like us to come home.
You may not know what tomorrow requires you to carry, but today you can surrender the one burden you were never meant to bear alone—your sin—and come to the Savior who carried the cross for you.
